artifact.working_title: The Grid Behind the AI Boom: IEA Demand, Bottlenecks, Prior Coverage
artifact.core_question: What does the latest IEA energy-and-AI update actually establish about data-centre electricity demand and bottlenecks, and how does that sit next to Nonsense’s earlier infrastructure, bill, and siting coverage?

research_brief.text: Usable IEA material is a news write-up of a new energy-and-AI analysis that builds on the April 2025 Energy and AI report. It says the field kept developing at speed, driven by data-centre investment, and that the report explores AI’s growing energy footprint, options for meeting data-centre power demand, and effects on affordability, security, and the wider economy. The headline states 2025 data-centre electricity use surged even with tightening bottlenecks and a scramble for solutions; the supplied body does not give totals or a bottleneck inventory. Prior Nonsense already treated AI as physical plant: a resource-and-power-cost story and a local data-centre siting/water fight.

research_cards.text: IEA issued a follow-on to its April 2025 Energy and AI report, tracking a fast-changing energy–AI relationship and close developments in the AI sector.

Headline: data-centre electricity use surged in 2025 even with tightening bottlenecks driving a scramble for solutions. Body: the analysis covers AI’s growing energy footprint, options for meeting data-centre power demand, and impacts on energy affordability, security, and the wider economy. Development continued at speed, driven by data-centre investment.
The only causal driver in the usable IEA excerpt is data-centre investment, not a finished generation or transmission buildout.

IEA frames the boom as an energy-system and economy problem. Prior Nonsense framed the same physical plant as household electricity-bill risk and local opposition, including water, not as a completed national demand forecast.
A recent prior big story already cast AI spending at country-GDP scale and called the chatbot a resource vampire tied to electricity bills—before this IEA update.

Separate IEA’s stated scope (footprint, power-supply options, affordability/security) from headline-only surge/bottleneck language, then add prior physical-constraint coverage without treating archive jokes as megawatt data.

conversation_questions: Which IEA claims live in the supplied body versus only in the 2025-surge/bottlenecks headline?
How should Episode 28’s electricity-bill and resource-vampire framing be used without turning it into a demand forecast?
Is Episode 29’s water and local-opposition fight the same constraint as grid bottlenecks, or a different force?
What competing readings does IEA itself name: power-supply options, affordability, security, wider economy?
What construction, generation, or transmission facts are still missing from usable evidence?

modular_outline.text: Establish the IEA follow-on: April 2025 Energy and AI predecessor; new analysis of a rapidly evolving energy–AI relationship.
State the report’s usable scope: growing energy footprint, options for meeting data-centre power demand, affordability, security, wider economy.
Handle the headline claim of a 2025 electricity surge plus tightening bottlenecks and a scramble for solutions, clearly marked as title-level unless more body text arrives.
Bring in prior infrastructure coverage: AI spending compared with country GDPs, electricity-bill cost, chatbot as resource vampire.
Add the adjacent siting/water constraint: local opposition and the Hillsborough, Oregon cluster of 18 active or under-construction sites.
Contrast interpretations that are in evidence: IEA’s economy/security frame versus local physical-plant pushback, without inventing rival forecasts.
Park nearby AI-jobs/headlines material that does not establish electricity or construction facts.

uncertainties_and_open_checks: Supplied IEA body has no kWh totals, regional split, or 2030 path.
Surge and bottleneck details are in the headline, not the excerpt.
No usable evidence on generation mix, interconnect queues, or build timelines.
Requested competing 2025–2030 forecasts are not in the supplied set.
Archive lines are comic and qualitative; do not treat them as load numbers.

A new report from the IEA assesses how the relationship between energy and artificial intelligence (AI) is evolving rapidly, drawing on the latest data and analysis and close tracking of technological and economic developments in the AI sector.Building on the IEA’s landmark Energy and AI report from April 2025, the new analysis published today finds that the field has continued to develop at speed.
